title: Understand Product Work
why: Product work connects decisions to user and business outcomes.
activity: Choose a product you use. Compare the responsibilities of a PM, Project Manager, and Product Owner using its context.
evidence: A one-page role comparison with examples.
reflection: Which responsibility interests you, and which assumption do you need to check?

title: Frame the Right Problem
why: A clear problem stops a team from treating a feature idea as a user need.
activity: Describe one real user, their context, the evidence for a problem, and a desired outcome. Separate observations from assumptions.
evidence: A problem statement with user, context, evidence, and outcome.
reflection: What would make you change your problem statement?

title: Connect User, Business, and Technology
why: Product decisions need to balance value, viability, and feasibility.
activity: Map your problem across user needs, business goals, and technical constraints. Explain one strategic choice and its trade-off.
evidence: A product triangle analysis and a strategic choice.
reflection: Which side of the triangle has the weakest evidence?

title: Conduct User Interviews
why: Listening helps challenge assumptions before you invest in a solution.
activity: Write neutral interview questions. Talk to at least three potential users with their consent. Avoid collecting identifying or sensitive details in your notes.
evidence: An interview guide and at least three anonymized interview notes.
reflection: Which answer surprised you, and what did you ask that might have led the participant?

title: Synthesize Insights
why: Individual observations become useful when you explain the pattern and its limits.
activity: Group observations from your interviews, identify patterns, and write opportunity statements. Keep contradictory findings.
evidence: Affinity groups, insights, and opportunity statements.
reflection: Which insight is supported by multiple observations?

title: Prioritize Opportunities
why: Limited time makes prioritization a decision with consequences.
activity: Compare at least three opportunities with a simple impact/effort matrix. Explain assumptions, confidence, and what you will defer.
evidence: A prioritization matrix and written rationale.
reflection: What evidence could reverse your priority order?

title: Write Requirements and Metrics
why: Clear requirements connect a proposed change to a measurable outcome.
activity: Write a mini PRD with problem, scope, non-goals, acceptance criteria, and success metrics. Include a baseline and a measurement plan.
evidence: A mini PRD, acceptance criteria, and success metrics.
reflection: Could a teammate understand what success looks like without asking you?

title: Build an Outcome Roadmap
why: A roadmap explains the outcomes you seek and the uncertainty between them.
activity: Create an outcome roadmap for your chosen problem. Include assumptions, dependencies, and a way to revisit priorities.
evidence: An outcome roadmap with assumptions and dependencies.
reflection: Which dependency could change your plan most?

title: Align a Cross-Functional Team
why: Shared decisions and visible risks make collaboration easier.
activity: Prepare a kickoff plan for a small team. Include responsibilities, a decision log, risks, and a concise stakeholder update. Ask a peer for feedback.
evidence: A kickoff plan, decision log, risk list, and stakeholder update.

title: Create a Product Case Study
why: A case study makes your reasoning reviewable rather than claiming expertise.
activity: Connect your problem, research, priorities, requirements, measurement plan, and reflection. Explain limits and decisions. Request feedback and document one improvement.
evidence: An end-to-end product case study and feedback reflection.
reflection: What did you learn, what remains unproven, and what would you do next?
